amendments.why: Rule 20's sentence marking a cleft or impersonal *it* `added` is written flat, and rule 40 already contradicts it for the very construction this chapter met twice: `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* puts the *it* inside the source unit. A pass reading rule 20 first would have marked the *it* of JOS.24.15 and JOS.24.16 `added` and left the morpheme that licenses it holding a bare adjective or a bare *Far*. The carve-out states the boundary this chapter used, gives it rule 31's subtraction test read for a frame, and closes by returning a cleft to the preceding sentences, so their force is untouched. Nothing else in the rule is altered.
amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **And where the ASV clefts a clause, the whole English frame goes the same way.** A cleft writes a dummy *it*, a copula, and a relative before the clause that carries the predication, and where the Hebrew writes a finite verb for that predication no morpheme answers to any of the three: the dummy and its copula are one `added` unit headed on the copula, and the cleft relative is its own `added` unit under rule 55, which marks a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause no written subordinator reaches. The copula is not this rule's construction-supplied one, because the test below asks which morpheme is there to carry the English and a clause whose predication a written verb already carries licenses no copula; and the relative is not rule 46's, because that rule supplies a relative to make a participle or a headless clause into a noun phrase, whereas a clefted nominal the ASV has already rendered is a written antecedent with a finite clause juxtaposed to it, which rule 46 excludes in its own terms. `לֹא־רַבִּים יֶחְכָּמוּ` → ***It is*** *not the great* ***that*** *are wise* gives *not* to the negative, *the great* to the substantival adjective under rule 46 and *are wise* to the finite verb, leaving *It is* and *that* `added`. Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **But an impersonal *it* the ASV writes inside one morpheme's own fixed English rendering is not such a dummy.** Where a Hebrew predicate word or interjection is rendered by an English expression the ASV never writes that word without — `רַע בְּעֵינֵי` → *it displease* and *it seem evil*, `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* — the *it* is part of that morpheme's own rendering, joins its unit and is never `added`, exactly as rule 30 gives the pronouns of `נָא` → *I beseech thee* to the particle and rule 55 gives the *As* of `חַי־אָנִי` → *As I live* to the adjective; rule 40 already reads `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* that way. Tell the two apart by the ASV's own use of the English, which is rule 31's test read for a frame rather than for a noun: where the ASV elsewhere writes that predicate's own word with nothing around it — *enough* for `רַב` — the frame is supplied and the preceding sentences govern, and where it never writes the word without the frame, the frame is the morpheme's. The unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme, so `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* heads on *Far*. This reaches a frame standing inside one morpheme's own rendering only: where every morpheme of the clause already holds its own English and the word is the opening of a cleft the ASV has built around it, the preceding sentences govern as before, and a referential subject pronoun answering to no morpheme at all is `added` on the terms rule 17 gives a supplied lexical subject noun. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **But the predicate morpheme that sentence looks for is one free to bear the copula, and a predicate that is itself a clause is not.** Where the predicate of such a tripartite clause is a relative or headless relative clause whose written finite verb already carries its own predication, no morpheme in it is available to take the matrix copula: assigning the word to that verb would leave one Hebrew verb holding two English clauses, which rule 17 refuses for the same reason in its matrix duration frame, and the resuming pronoun is then the clause's only overt anchor and takes the copula, exactly as an explicit subject does where the predicate is wholly elided. `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` → *That which hath been* ***is*** *that which shall be* gives *is* to `הוּא`, while `שֶׁ` keeps the *that which* rule 46's first rider gives it and `יִּהְיֶה` keeps its own *shall be*. Read what the predicate is before applying the preceding paragraph: a nominal, adjectival or prepositional predicate is free to take the copula and the pronoun is `unrepresented` as before, and one chapter may write both shapes, as ECC.1.9 and ECC.1.17 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.

conventions: Impersonal English *it*. Where it stands inside the fixed English rendering of a Hebrew predicate word or interjection that the ASV never writes without it, it joins that morpheme's unit: רַע → *it seem evil* at 24.15, following rule 40's decided *it displease*, and חָלִילָה → *Far be it* at 24.16, headed on *Far*. Where every morpheme of the clause already holds its own English and the word merely opens a cleft the ASV has built, it is `added`: *he it is that brought us up* at 24.17, where הוּא keeps its own *he*, the article keeps the relative *that* under rule 41 and the participle keeps the copula. A referential supplied subject that no morpheme in the verse denotes is `added` on the ordinary terms, as *We* is at 24.22, both occurrences of אַתֶּם having already been spent.

*out of* after a verb of bringing. Where מִן stands in the clause it takes the whole *out of*, headed on *out* (24.6, 24.10, 24.17, 24.32), and the hiphil keeps only its own verb together with any second particle, as *brought ... up* does at 24.17 and 24.32. Where no preposition stands, the particle is the verb's own under rule 44, as *I brought you out* is at 24.5. Read whether the preposition is present before placing the word: what differs between 24.5 and 24.6 is the morpheme, not the English.

amended.text: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **And where the ASV clefts a clause, the whole English frame goes the same way.** A cleft writes a dummy *it*, a copula, and a relative before the clause that carries the predication, and where the Hebrew writes a finite verb for that predication no morpheme answers to any of the three: the dummy and its copula are one `added` unit headed on the copula, and the cleft relative is its own `added` unit under rule 55, which marks a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause no written subordinator reaches. The copula is not this rule's construction-supplied one, because the test below asks which morpheme is there to carry the English and a clause whose predication a written verb already carries licenses no copula; and the relative is not rule 46's, because that rule supplies a relative to make a participle or a headless clause into a noun phrase, whereas a clefted nominal the ASV has already rendered is a written antecedent with a finite clause juxtaposed to it, which rule 46 excludes in its own terms. `לֹא־רַבִּים יֶחְכָּמוּ` → ***It is*** *not the great* ***that*** *are wise* gives *not* to the negative, *the great* to the substantival adjective under rule 46 and *are wise* to the finite verb, leaving *It is* and *that* `added`. Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **But an impersonal *it* the ASV writes inside one morpheme's own fixed English rendering is not such a dummy.** Where a Hebrew predicate word or interjection is rendered by an English expression the ASV never writes that word without — `רַע בְּעֵינֵי` → *it displease* and *it seem evil*, `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* — the *it* is part of that morpheme's own rendering, joins its unit and is never `added`, exactly as rule 30 gives the pronouns of `נָא` → *I beseech thee* to the particle and rule 55 gives the *As* of `חַי־אָנִי` → *As I live* to the adjective; rule 40 already reads `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* that way. Tell the two apart by the ASV's own use of the English, which is rule 31's test read for a frame rather than for a noun: where the ASV elsewhere writes that predicate's own word with nothing around it — *enough* for `רַב` — the frame is supplied and the preceding sentences govern, and where it never writes the word without the frame, the frame is the morpheme's. The unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme, so `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* heads on *Far*. This reaches a frame standing inside one morpheme's own rendering only: where every morpheme of the clause already holds its own English and the word is the opening of a cleft the ASV has built around it, the preceding sentences govern as before, and a referential subject pronoun answering to no morpheme at all is `added` on the terms rule 17 gives a supplied lexical subject noun. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **But the predicate morpheme that sentence looks for is one free to bear the copula, and a predicate that is itself a clause is not.** Where the predicate of such a tripartite clause is a relative or headless relative clause whose written finite verb already carries its own predication, no morpheme in it is available to take the matrix copula: assigning the word to that verb would leave one Hebrew verb holding two English clauses, which rule 17 refuses for the same reason in its matrix duration frame, and the resuming pronoun is then the clause's only overt anchor and takes the copula, exactly as an explicit subject does where the predicate is wholly elided. `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` → *That which hath been* ***is*** *that which shall be* gives *is* to `הוּא`, while `שֶׁ` keeps the *that which* rule 46's first rider gives it and `יִּהְיֶה` keeps its own *shall be*. Read what the predicate is before applying the preceding paragraph: a nominal, adjectival or prepositional predicate is free to take the copula and the pronoun is `unrepresented` as before, and one chapter may write both shapes, as ECC.1.9 and ECC.1.17 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amended.why: Rule 20's sentence marking a cleft or impersonal *it* `added` is written flat, and rule 40 already contradicts it for the very construction this chapter met twice: `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* puts the *it* inside the source unit. A pass reading rule 20 first would have marked the *it* of JOS.24.15 and JOS.24.16 `added` and left the morpheme that licenses it holding a bare adjective or a bare *Far*. The carve-out states the boundary this chapter used, gives it rule 31's subtraction test read for a frame, and closes by returning a cleft to the preceding sentences, so their force is untouched. Nothing else in the rule is altered.

report: All 65 candidate groups read. Every multi-treatment bucket is the ASV writing different English for one morpheme, which the contract reads off the printed translation: the waw's connectives, the prepositions' varying English, and the proper-name buckets that differ only by whether an *of* was written. No bucket holds one construction analysed two ways.

Preposition plus construct noun is the chapter's most repeated fused/split pair, and it divides exactly on rule 30's condition. בְּ/מֵ + עֵבֶר fuses to a bare *beyond* at 24.2, 24.8, 24.14 and 24.15 (the verbless clause's copula joining the fused unit at 24.15) and splits at 24.3, where the ASV writes *from beyond*; לִפְנֵי fuses at 24.1 and 24.12 while מִפְּנֵי splits as *from before* at 24.8, 24.12 and 24.18; בְּקֶרֶב fuses to *among* at 24.23 and splits at 24.5 and 24.17 where the ASV writes *in* and *through* beside *the midst*; בְּעֵינֵי fuses to *unto* at 24.15 while לְעֵינֵי splits at 24.17 as *in our sight*. None owes a patch.

Determiner counting is uniform. An anarthrous rectum leaves the phrase's one *the* to the article with the construct bare (24.23, 24.32); an arthrous rectum gives each word the *the* standing before it (24.8, 24.12, 24.15, 24.31); with no article morpheme the construct takes a supplied *the*, one per level in a multi-level chain (24.26). A written demonstrative goes to the demonstrative pronoun with the articles unrepresented (24.17, 24.25, 24.26, 24.27, 24.29) and to the article itself where no pronoun stands (24.15 הַיּוֹם → *this day*).

Read end to end for what the lemma table cannot see, the supplied subject pronouns are the only real question and the difference is licensed. The impersonal *it* joins the source unit at 24.15 (רַע → *it seem evil*, which is rule 40's own decided *it displease*) and at 24.16 (חָלִילָה → *Far be it*, a formula the ASV never writes without its frame), and is `added` at 24.17, where every morpheme of the clause already holds its own English and the word merely opens a cleft. Recorded as a convention; rule 20's flat sentence on the impersonal *it*, which rule 40 already contradicts, is amended rather than left standing for the next chapter to read first.

BSB: none of the disagreements is an error. The Td, To and R runs are the documented convention differences — articles the ASV does not write, the object marker, and prepositions the ASV's recasting silences. The singletons are the same thing one at a time: a paragogic nun at 24.15 and 24.27, a paragogic he at 24.16, an apodosis waw the ASV opens bare at 24.7, the waw of וְאִם at 24.15 whose one written connective the second אִם holds, a preposition dropped in *that day* at 24.25, and the second relative of a coordinated pair at 24.31.

The two large-source-unit candidates (24.13 unit 6, 24.17 unit 41) are the three-morpheme *whereon* and *wherein* fusions rule 22 names outright, and both suffixes agree with and denote their antecedents. The three underdetermined ketiv/qere units at 24.3, 24.8 and 24.15 each retain a reading the ASV renders, so rule 53 is not reached.
